title: Raga or popular tune
hook: some sing kirtan strictly in ragas, others in simpler tunes; both are loved

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rababi families, who sang the Gurus' hymns on a Muslim musician's strings. Your line was mardana's heirs. Whose music did you trace back to someone? Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

Two gurdwaras, a few streets apart, on the same evening. In the first, a raagi sits with a harmonium and a tabla player and opens a hymn slowly, notes rising in a set order, a mood held for a long while before the words even begin. In the second, a group of teenagers sings the same hymn to a simple tune, the kind you could hum after hearing it once, and the whole hall sings back. Both are kirtan. Both are the Gurus' words. So which way is right? Sikhs have argued about it with real care, and today's title is the question: raga or popular tune.
screen: `SAME HYMN, TWO HALLS.` → `A SLOW RAGA. A SIMPLE TUNE.` → `WHICH WAY IS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: First, the book itself is built on ragas. Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the hymns are gathered under raga headings: Sri Raag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on through the book. A raga is more than a scale. It's a set of notes, a way of moving between them, and a mood the music is meant to carry. So some Sikhs say plainly: if a Guru set a hymn in a raga, sing it in that raga. The music is part of the message, and changing it loses something the Guru chose. Second, the other side. Others say what matters is that the words reach people. A simple tune lets a whole hall sing. A child learns a hymn by heart on the way home. A newcomer can join on the very first night. For them, a tune that opens the door is doing the Guru's work. Third, what the scripture says about ragas themselves. In a var in Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das names Sri Raag as the finest of the ragas, and then adds the condition in the same breath. In paraphrase: it is finest if, through it, a person holds love for the truth. Even the praise of a raga is tied to love. A perfect raga sung without that, by this line, misses the point. Fourth, both are loved. Some gurdwaras keep strict raga kirtan; others sing in simpler tunes; some sangats hear both in the same week. Those who keep the ragas guard something precious. Those who sing simply open a door. The line from Sri Raag sits over both of them: the music serves the love, not the other way around.
screen: `THE BOOK IS BUILT ON RAGAS.` · `A TUNE THAT OPENS THE DOOR.` · `FINEST, IF IT HOLDS LOVE.` · `BOTH ARE LOVED.` · then, large: `THE MUSIC SERVES THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to both styles. Settle, and breathe. If you can, play a short stretch of raga kirtan, and then a hymn sung to a simple tune. If you can't right now, recall one slow piece of music you know and one you could hum after a single hearing. Don't rank them. Just notice what each one asks of you: the slow one asks you to wait, the simple one invites you to join. Let both have a place. The bell holds the time.
Raga or popular tune. The question of how to sing the Gurus' hymns: in the ragas the book names, or in simple tunes a whole hall can sing. Sikhs hold both. Today's word.
Your line: both are loved. Today, when you meet two ways of doing one good thing, find what each one protects before you pick a side. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.
